questions.q: What is electromagnetic induction, as Faraday discovered it in August 1831?
options: The force a current-carrying conductor feels when placed in an external magnetic field
The generation of an emf and/or an electric current through the use of a magnetic field
The magnetic field produced around a wire whenever a steady current flows in it
The alignment of magnetic domains when iron is placed near a permanent magnet
questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction is the generation of an emf and/or electric current through the use of a magnetic field. Option A describes the motor effect (Faraday's 1821 discovery), which is a different phenomenon; induction is the reverse idea of getting electricity from magnetism.

questions.q: In the relationship for magnetic flux, what does the term 'magnetic flux density' actually refer to, and in what unit is magnetic flux measured?
options: Flux density is the flux \(\phi_B\) itself, measured in tesla
Flux density is the magnetic field strength \(B\), measured in tesla (Wb m⁻²); flux \(\phi_B\) is measured in weber
Flux density is the area \(A\) of the coil, measured in weber per metre
Flux density is the rate of change of flux, measured in weber per second
questions.explanation: The strength of a magnetic field, B, is also known as the magnetic flux density — the amount of flux passing through a unit area — and it is measured in tesla (Wb m⁻²). The flux \(\phi_B = B_\perp A\) itself is measured in weber. Confusing flux density (the tesla quantity) with flux (the weber quantity) is a classic exam trap.

questions.q: Which statement correctly states Faraday's Law of Induction?
options: The induced emf in a circuit equals the magnetic flux through the circuit
The induced emf in a circuit is equal in magnitude to the rate at which the magnetic flux through the circuit is changing with time
The induced emf in a circuit is proportional to the strength of the magnetic field threading the coil
The induced emf in a circuit equals the area of the coil times the magnetic field strength
questions.explanation: Faraday's Law states the induced emf is equal in magnitude to the rate at which the magnetic flux through the circuit is changing with time, written \(\varepsilon = -\dfrac{\Delta\phi_B}{\Delta t}\). It is the rate of change of flux that matters — a large but steady flux gives zero emf.

questions.q: A single rectangular loop measuring 0.25 m by 0.3 m takes 2.0 s to fully enter a perpendicular magnetic field of 0.66 T strength. Calculate the magnitude of the induced emf in the loop.
working: Change in flux (field perpendicular, so \(\phi_B = BA\)): \(\Delta\phi_B = (BA)_{final} - (BA)_{initial} = (0.66 \times 0.075) - (0 \times 0.075)\)
Magnitude of the induced emf \(= 0.025\,\mathrm{V}\) (25 mV). The minus sign indicates the induced emf opposes the change in flux (Lenz's Law).
questions.explanation: Always take change in flux as final minus initial; the loop starts outside the field so the initial flux is zero. With one turn the emf is 0.025 V — and with 200 turns it would be 200 times larger, about 5 V, for the same flux change.

questions.q: A spring bent into a circle of radius 5.0 cm sits in a magnetic field of strength 0.55 T (field perpendicular to the loop, single turn). It is released and contracts to a circle of radius 3.0 cm in 0.15 seconds. Calculate the magnitude of the induced emf.
working: Convert radii to metres before squaring: \(0.05\,\mathrm{m}\) and \(0.03\,\mathrm{m}\).
Magnitude of the induced emf \(\approx 0.018\,\mathrm{V}\) (18 mV).
questions.explanation: Here the field B stays constant at 0.55 T the whole time — it is the area A that changes, so the flux changes (lever A of the BAT). This proves a constant field does not mean constant flux: you can induce an emf by changing the area alone.

questions.q: If a coil has n turns of wire instead of one, how is the emf induced by a given change in magnetic flux threading the coil affected?
options: The emf is unchanged, because flux does not depend on the number of turns
The emf is n times greater, because every turn has the same emf induced and the turns add in series
The emf is divided by n, because the flux is shared between the turns
The emf is n squared times greater, because area scales with turns
questions.explanation: If a coil has n turns, the emf induced by a change in flux is n times greater than for a single turn, giving \(\varepsilon = -\dfrac{N\Delta\phi_B}{\Delta t}\). Each turn encloses the same changing flux and the turns are wired in series, so their emfs add like batteries in a row.

questions.q: From memory: in Faraday's moving-magnet experiments, what happens to the induced current when the magnet is held stationary near the coil, and what does the magnet's speed control?
keyPoints: When the magnet is held without moving near the end of the coil, the galvanometer needle stays at the central point — no current is induced.
A current is induced only while the magnet is moving (approaching or being taken away), i.e. only while the flux is changing.
The magnitude of the induced current depends on the speed of the magnet: a slow magnet induces a small current, a fast magnet induces a larger current.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that a stationary magnet induces nothing and that faster motion induces a larger current, grade yourself Good or Easy. The deep point is that only a changing flux induces — a strong but steady field does nothing.

questions.q: From memory: explain why an induced current can occur in a solid sheet of metal moving through a magnetic field even though it has no wire loops, and name these currents.
keyPoints: Induced currents do not occur only in coils and wires; they also occur when a conductor moves in an external magnetic field or a metal object is subjected to a changing magnetic field.
The changing flux through the body of the metal induces an emf, which drives currents that swirl in closed loops through the bulk of the sheet — these are eddy currents.
Eddy currents are an application of Lenz's Law: the magnetic fields they set up oppose the change, so the induced force always opposes the motion of the sheet.
questions.explanation: The marked trap is claiming 'no wire loops, so no induction'. A conductor plus a changing flux is all you need; the current just circulates through the solid metal as eddy currents that oppose the motion.

questions.q: Using the memory hook 'swing the BAT', which three changes can each induce an emf by changing the flux \(\phi_B = BA\cos\theta\) through a coil?
options: Change the resistance, the current, or the voltage of the coil
Change the field strength B, the area A, or the angle \(\theta\) between the field and the coil's normal
Change the temperature, the material, or the thickness of the wire
Change the number of turns, the time, or the speed of the magnet only
questions.explanation: Because \(\phi_B = BA\cos\theta\), changing any one of B, A or \(\theta\) changes the flux and induces an emf — 'swing the BAT'. All three run through the identical machinery: a changing flux induces an emf, regardless of which lever caused the change.

questions.q: Explain why an EMF is induced when a bar magnet is moved into a solenoid, and state the condition required for a current to flow. (4 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: As the magnet moves into the solenoid, the magnetic field through the coil increases, so the magnetic flux through the coil increases. By Faraday's Law of electromagnetic induction, this change in flux induces an EMF in the coil, equal to the number of turns times the rate of change of flux, so a faster-moving magnet or more turns gives a larger EMF. This induced EMF then drives an induced current around the coil — but only if the coil forms a complete circuit. If the circuit is open, the EMF is still induced but no current flows.

criteria.descriptor: States the magnet's motion increases the field, so the flux through the coil changes.
Applies Faraday's Law: the changing flux induces an EMF equal to N × rate of change of flux.
Links faster motion / more turns to a larger EMF.
States a current flows only if the coil forms a complete circuit; otherwise an EMF exists but no current.

questions.explanation: Run the three-step chain — 'Flux, EMF, Current, if Closed' — and keep EMF and current strictly distinct. Collapsing it to 'the magnet makes a current' is the band-four answer and leaves marks on the table.
